name: แนวโน้มที่จะเพิ่มน้ำหนักหรือกักเก็บน้ำ
preview_text: น้ำหนักที่เพิ่มขึ้นและอาการบวมใน TCM ไม่ใช่แค่เรื่องแคลอรี่เท่านั้น แต่ยังเป็นสัญญาณว่าระบบการเผาผลาญของเหลวในร่างกายของคุณหยุดชะงัก ชนิดของความหนัก การเคลือบลิ้น และสิ่งที่ทำให้...
categories: ["ปัญหาเรื่องน้ำหนัก", "อาการบวมและการเก็บของเหลว"]
synonyms: ["Weight gain from fluid retention", "Weight gain or mild puffiness", "Tendency to gain weight or retain water easily"]
conventional_description:
In Western medicine, a tendency to gain weight easily or retain water is often attributed to fluid retention (edema), which can result from high sodium intake, hormonal fluctuations (such as premenstrual water retention), certain medications, or underlying conditions affecting the heart, kidneys, or thyroid. Mild puffiness, bloating, and a feeling of heaviness are common complaints, and diagnosis typically involves a physical exam, blood tests, and sometimes imaging to rule out organ dysfunction.
When no serious cause is found, the condition is often labeled idiopathic edema, and management focuses on dietary and lifestyle adjustments.
conventional_treatments:
Standard approaches include reducing dietary sodium, increasing water intake to flush excess fluids, and using compression stockings for leg swelling. Diuretics (water pills) may be prescribed for more significant fluid retention, though they are generally used short-term due to side effects like electrolyte imbalances.
For hormone-related water weight, hormonal therapies or lifestyle changes may be recommended. When an underlying condition like heart failure or kidney disease is present, treatment targets that primary issue.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, a tendency to gain weight or retain water is not a single condition but a sign that the body's fluid metabolism has stalled.
The Spleen is the primary organ responsible for transforming food and drink into Qi and clear fluids, and for transporting them to where they're needed. When the Spleen is weakened - often by poor diet, overwork, or stress - it fails to manage fluids properly, and dampness accumulates. This dampness makes you feel heavy and puffy, and it shows up as easy weight gain and water retention, especially after eating or during humid weather.
If dampness lingers, it can thicken into Phlegm, a stickier, more stubborn substance that creates a feeling of being weighed down and a foggy head.
The Kidney also plays a crucial role: its Yang energy warms and transforms fluids throughout the body. When Kidney Yang is deficient, water metabolism slows to a crawl, leading to a waterlogged kind of weight gain, often with lower-body puffiness and coldness. Less commonly, dampness can combine with heat, creating a pattern of Damp-Heat that feels heavy yet hot, with a bitter taste and yellow tongue coating.
This is why two people with the same complaint of puffiness and weight gain may be treated very differently. One might have a pale, swollen tongue with a white greasy coating and loose stools (Spleen Deficiency with Dampness), while another has a thick, greasy coating and a feeling of mental fog (Damp-Phlegm).
A third might have a deep, weak pulse and a cold lower back (Kidney Yang Deficiency). TCM treatment aims to identify and correct the specific underlying imbalance, not just drain the fluid.
classical_quote: 「Dampness prevails, then the skin is not firm, and the flesh is soft; when dampness attacks, the patient feels heavy and swollen.」
classical_translation: "When dampness predominates, the skin loses its firmness and the flesh becomes soft. As dampness strikes, the person experiences a sensation of heaviness and swelling."
classical_source:
Su Wen (Plain Questions)  ,  Chapter 43: Bi Syndrome 									·
More references
tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner begins by asking about the quality of your weight gain and any fluid retention. Puffiness that shifts during the day, digestive sluggishness, and a feeling of heaviness all point toward dampness. The tongue and pulse then help separate the patterns, because a pale, swollen tongue with a white greasy coating and a slippery pulse tell a very different story from a red tongue with a yellow greasy coating.
When Spleen Deficiency with Dampness is the main picture, the person often feels bloated after eating, tires easily, and has loose stools. The weight gain is soft and puffy rather than firm. The tongue is pale and swollen with a white, greasy coat, and the pulse feels slippery yet slightly weak. All signs confirm that the Spleen is not transforming fluids properly.
If dampness has congealed into Damp-Phlegm, the heaviness is more pronounced and the coating becomes thicker and stickier. A person may notice more mucus, a foggy head, and a persistent feeling of being weighed down. The tongue is swollen with a thick, greasy coating, and the pulse is full and slippery. This pattern points to a deeper, more stubborn metabolic stagnation.
Less commonly, Kidney Yang Deficiency with Water overflowing adds a layer of cold. Here the puffiness is often worse in the lower body, accompanied by cold limbs and lower back weakness. The tongue is pale, swollen, and wet, and the pulse is deep and slow.
In rare cases Damp-Heat in the Stomach and Spleen mixes heat with dampness, bringing a bitter taste, sticky yellow coating, and a rapid, slippery pulse - a warmer, more irritated picture.

patterns.symptoms: ["Feeling of heaviness in the body and limbs", "Abdominal bloating that gets worse after eating", "Loose or unformed stools", "Fatigue and lack of energy", "Puffy face and limbs, especially in the morning", "Drowsiness after meals"]
patterns.worse_with: Overeating or heavy meals, Cold, raw foods and iced drinks, Damp, humid weather, Sedentary lifestyle, Stress and worry
patterns.better_with: Warm, cooked meals, Gentle exercise like walking, Warm, dry environment, Adequate rest and sleep
patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen is your body's engine for transforming food and drink into Qi and clear fluids. When it becomes weak, it can't properly process and transport fluids, so dampness builds up inside. This dampness makes you feel heavy and puffy, and it shows up as easy weight gain and water retention, especially around the belly.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen with teeth marks, and a white greasy coating. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and slowed-down (Huan), soft and lacking force, especially at the right wrist position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen thrives on warmth and gentle activity. Cold, raw foods and overeating overwhelm its digestive fire, creating dampness that leads to puffiness and weight gain. Warm, cooked meals and moderate exercise support Spleen function, helping it transform fluids and prevent accumulation. Stress knots Liver Qi, which then attacks the Spleen, so staying calm also protects digestion.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked meals like soups and stews, and avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that burden the Spleen. Incorporate barley (Yi Yi Ren), lotus seeds, and Chinese yam into your diet. Gentle daily exercise like walking or yoga helps Qi flow and dries dampness.

patterns.worse_with: Damp, humid weather, Sedentary lifestyle, Rich, greasy, or fried foods, Stress and worry, Cold, raw foods and iced drinks
patterns.better_with: Warm, dry environment, Gentle exercise like walking, Warm, cooked meals, Avoiding greasy, sweet, and cold foods, Keeping the abdomen warm
patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen fails to transform fluids properly, dampness builds up and eventually congeals into a thicker, stickier substance called Phlegm. This Phlegm-Damp collects in the tissues, creating a heavy, bloated feeling and making it very easy to gain weight or retain water, especially around the abdomen and limbs. The metabolic engine becomes sluggish, so even normal eating can lead to puffiness and a sense of being 'waterlogged.'
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with scalloped teeth marks, thick white greasy coating that looks oily, wet surface. Pulse: slippery (滑 Huá), and may be soggy in the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Phlegm is a heavy, cold, and stagnant pathogen that thrives when the Spleen is weak and fluids are not moved. Damp weather and sedentary habits further slow down Qi and allow phlegm to accumulate, while greasy, cold foods directly burden the Spleen and create more dampness. On the other hand, warmth, movement, and light, cooked meals gently activate the Spleen's transforming function, helping to 'dry out' the internal environment and flush out retained fluids.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on warm, cooked foods like soups and stews, and favor barley, job's tears (coix seed), and lightly cooked vegetables. Avoid cold drinks, dairy, sweets, and greasy fried foods, which create more dampness. Gentle daily movement like walking or yoga helps the Spleen move fluids and prevent phlegm from settling.

patterns.pattern_name: Kidney Yang Deficiency with Water overflowing
patterns.symptoms: ["Swelling of legs and ankles that worsens with standing", "Feeling of cold, especially in the lower back and limbs", "Scanty, clear urination", "Soreness and weakness of the lower back", "Abdominal bloating and loose stools"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold, damp weather, Overwork and exhaustion, Cold, raw foods and iced drinks, Prolonged standing
patterns.better_with: Warmth (heating pad on lower back), Adequate rest and sleep, Warm, cooked meals, Gentle exercise like walking
patterns.why_this_happens: Kidney Yang is the body's pilot light - it warms and transforms all fluids. When it weakens, water metabolism stalls and fluids accumulate rather than being moved out as urine. This leads to a heavy, waterlogged kind of weight gain, especially in the lower body, along with puffiness and swelling that feels cold to the touch.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and teeth-marked with a white slippery coating; the surface looks excessively wet. Pulse: deep (沉 chén), slow (迟 chí), and weak (弱 ruò), especially faint at the rear (Kidney) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and overwork drain the Kidney's warming Yang, freezing fluid metabolism and worsening water retention. Warmth, rest, and warm foods conserve and replenish that Yang, helping the body transform and excrete accumulated fluids. Gentle movement supports circulation without depleting energy, while prolonged standing allows fluids to pool in the legs.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews; avoid icy drinks, raw salads, and dairy which chill the body. Keep your lower back and feet warm, and avoid sitting on cold surfaces. Gentle daily movement like walking helps activate Yang, but stop before exhaustion.

patterns.why_this_happens: When dampness and heat combine in the Stomach and Spleen, the Spleen's ability to transform and transport fluids is impaired. This leads to an accumulation of dampness and water, causing a heavy, puffy feeling and weight gain that is difficult to lose. The heat component makes the dampness stickier and more stubborn, often adding signs like a bitter taste and sticky bowel movements.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly swollen with teeth marks, thick yellow greasy coating especially at the centre and root. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and rapid (Shu), often slippery (Hua).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-heat arises when the Spleen is overwhelmed by greasy, sweet, or spicy foods, creating internal dampness that ferments into heat. Avoiding these foods reduces the damp-heat load, while cooling, light meals help clear heat and drain dampness. Moderate exercise moves Qi and assists the Spleen in transforming dampness, and a dry environment prevents external dampness from adding to the internal burden.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid rich, greasy, and spicy foods that add heat and dampness. Focus on light, cooling meals with vegetables like bitter gourd and cucumber, and include barley (coix) to drain dampness. Gentle, regular exercise like walking helps Qi move and dries internal dampness.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help with water retention?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture stimulates points that strengthen the Spleen, promote urination, and move stagnant fluids. Many people notice less bloating and a lighter feeling after just a few sessions, though lasting change requires a series of treatments combined with herbs and diet.

faqs.question: Will Chinese herbs make me lose water weight quickly?
faqs.answer: Chinese herbs are not quick-fix diuretics. They work by restoring your body's ability to process fluids on its own, so weight loss tends to be gradual and sustainable rather than a sudden drop. You may notice improved digestion and less puffiness before the scale moves significantly.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet for TCM to work?
faqs.answer: Yes, diet is central to TCM treatment for dampness. Cold, raw, and greasy foods burden the Spleen and create more dampness, so avoiding them while eating warm, cooked meals dramatically speeds up your progress. Your practitioner will give you specific guidance, but the general rules are simple and make a big difference.

faqs.question: Is it safe to take Chinese herbs if I'm already on a diuretic?
faqs.answer: It's important to tell both your TCM practitioner and your prescribing doctor. Some herbs have mild diuretic effects, and combining them with water pills could lead to excessive fluid loss or electrolyte imbalances. Your TCM practitioner can adjust the formula accordingly and may recommend monitoring your blood pressure and kidney function.

faqs.question: Can TCM help if my water retention is hormonal, like before my period?
faqs.answer: Yes. TCM views premenstrual bloating as a sign of Liver Qi stagnation and Spleen dampness. By smoothing the Liver and strengthening the Spleen with herbs and acupuncture timed to your cycle, many women find significant relief from monthly puffiness and weight gain.

research.title: Acupuncture for obesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: Meta-analysis of 31 RCTs found acupuncture significantly reduced body weight and BMI compared to sham or no treatment, but study quality varied.
research.periodical: Cho SH, Lee JS, Thabane L, Lee J. Acupuncture for obesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis. International Journal of Obesity. 2009;33(2):183-196.

research.title: Effects of electroacupuncture in reducing weight and waist circumference in obese women: a randomized crossover trial
research.description: RCT of 54 obese women showed electroacupuncture significantly reduced body weight and waist circumference compared to control after 6 weeks.
research.periodical: Hsu CH, Hwang KC, Chao CL, Lin JG, Kao ST, Chou P. Effects of electroacupuncture in reducing weight and waist circumference in obese women: a randomized crossover trial. International Journal of Obesity. 2005;29(11):1379-1384.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for chronic venous insufficiency
research.description: Cochrane systematic review found some herbal medicines may improve leg swelling and pain, but evidence was insufficient to recommend any specific herb.
research.periodical: Martinez-Zapata MJ, Vernooij RW, Uriona Tuma SM, et al. Chinese herbal medicine for chronic venous insufficiency. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016, Issue 5. Art. No.: CD006650.
